meta.title: Sleep History Logic Map
meta.subtitle: Does sleep keep an internal history, and how does it cope with disturbance?
meta.scope: 6 implanted rats (SF07–SF12) in an outdoor paddock, 2026-08-30 → 09-11 19:40 (the five females after that are excluded); 169 sessions → 129 records, 1227 h. Automatic 1-s scores (FINAL); no manual epoch scoring (κ).
meta.focus_note: Link being built: an individual's own sleep history ↔ who keeps sleeping and who wakes in the same group event

nodes.title: Does sleep keep an internal history, and does it reorganise NREM/REM to cope with disturbance?
nodes.text: Core question (the user, 2026-10-08). The direction to connect: an individual's own sleep history, and why in the same group event some animals keep sleeping while others wake. Framing agreed 2026-10-07: an internal rule that organises sleep states, carries history and is updated during wakes; not a fixed timetable; it has to survive interruptions.

nodes.title: Sleep is interrupted all the time, yet daily amounts are regular
nodes.text: Over 08-31 → 09-06 (all 6 rats): NREM 9.7 ± 0.2 h and REM 1.8 ± 0.1 h per 24 h; REM 15.9 % of sleep. 82 % of REM-to-REM intervals contain some wake; the median wake bout lasts 23 s.

nodes.title: Internal regulation that carries history
nodes.text: Sleep follows rules that carry a short summary of recent sleep (the PI's scheduling hypothesis as reframed with the user, 2026-10-07). Pattern level: says nothing about the neural implementation. How wakes update the summary is a separate, candidate question (Q4).

sources.anchor: internal rule that organises sleep states

nodes.title: No carried history: clock, conditions and the current state are enough
nodes.text: Transitions follow the circadian clock, the conditions and the current state only (a fixed timetable or memoryless switching). The null against every history claim.

changes.what: Source re-cited after the audit's #21 wording fix (commit a3ca36e).

nodes.title: Stage trade-off (the PI's first formulation): one stage longer → the other shorter
nodes.text: Within a sleep cycle, stages are allocated against each other like jobs on a processor: a longer REM shortens the following NREM, or a longer NREM shortens the next REM.

nodes.title: Sleep budget: deviations are made up later (hours to a day)
nodes.text: A shortfall of REM or NREM is followed by a surplus, so amounts are balanced over hours or over the 24 h (homeostatic payback). Shown in the literature only after deprivation, never in undisturbed data.

sources.anchor: A budget has been shown only after deprivation

nodes.title: A neural scheduler allocates NREM and REM time
nodes.text: The mechanistic reading: a brain circuit schedules sleep states like a job scheduler. Needs an intervention and neural content; natural data can only test predictive dependence on history.

nodes.title: #21 The brain schedules sleep — unresolved by design
nodes.text: Natural data with no intervention beyond the battery rounds cannot show a scheduling mechanism. Allowed (corrected 2026-10-09): history-dependent, interruption-sensitive rules that reproduce the daily totals without a daily budget, consistent with an internal regulation of REM entry rather than a fixed timetable; a REM repayment only after handled interruptions (candidate); no day-to-day balance shown.
nodes.allowed: The data show history-dependent, interruption-sensitive rules — and daily REM and NREM totals that those rules reproduce without a daily budget — consistent with an internal regulation of REM entry rather than a fixed timetable. A repayment of REM has been seen only after handled interruptions (candidate); no day-to-day balance was shown.
nodes.forbidden: Mechanistic 'scheduler' wording. 'Balancing / balanced over the day' (#13 withdrawn).

changes.what: Allowed wording corrected by the claim audit (commit a3ca36e) after the Fable conflict review: 'balancing over the day' removed and now forbidden (c.balance_wording resolved). Old allowed wording: 'The data show history-dependent, interruption-sensitive rules and balancing over the day, consistent with an internal regulation of sleep, not a fixed timetable.'

nodes.title: v1 #11 The PI's scheduling mechanism — not testable with this design
nodes.text: The analysis measures statistical dependence of scored-state timing on history, not allocation.

nodes.title: Rules that carry history: yes. A fixed timetable: no. A scheduler mechanism: not testable here.
nodes.text: Established: sleep follows rules that carry history. REM becomes more likely the more NREM has built up since the last REM; brief awakenings do not erase that build-up; the night limits how often REM starts, not how long it lasts. Candidate: a long wake pushes the next REM back without resuming the earlier progress; sleep is balanced between night and day. Not shown: a fixed timetable, minute-for-minute compensation, outside causes of awakenings, a mechanism.

changes.what: Superseded by j.core.r2: the night-day 'balance' (#13) was withdrawn as a cohort drift (#30). Source re-pointed to the claim rows (the r1 synthesis was rewritten in the audit on 2026-10-08).

nodes.title: Organising idea: only REM entry is regulated — by the count since the last REM and a smooth daily curve
nodes.text: Proposed by the logic audit (Fable, 2026-10-08) and kept in the claim audit's synthesis as an interpretation: REM entry is the regulated knob (#14: the night limits entry, not duration), REM duration and REM exits follow no history, and daily totals are regular because the inputs are regular, not because a budget is enforced. #40 is consistent with it (the generative model has history on REM entry only), but REM-bout duration and REM exits were never tested for regulation (step F H7, H8): stays proposed.

sources.anchor: only REM entry is regulated, by

nodes.title: Rules that carry history: yes. No day-to-day balance (a drift). Organising idea under test: only REM entry is regulated.
nodes.text: Established: REM entry tracks the NREM accumulated since the last REM; brief awakenings do not erase that history; the night limits how often REM starts, not how long it lasts; over the 12 days all rats moved sleep from night into day (#30, a drift, not a balance). Candidate: a wake ≥ 7 min is not resumed; at night longer wakes delay REM further; the night lowers REM entry even after equally short wakes; REM missed before a morning round is repaid, specifically REM. Interpretation to test (the plan's scheduler model): only REM entry is regulated, by a count, a day/night gain and perhaps a slow REM deficit. Not shown: a day-to-day 24-h balance, a fixed timetable, an NREM rebound proportional to wake length, outside causes of awakenings, a mechanism.

changes.what: Step A: #6a (not resumed) becomes Established; #14b and #10 re-evidenced (A3 PARTIAL, A4 PASS on fixed thresholds).
Step B: one count since the last REM, emptied by REM and fading over a wake (τ_w 5–10 min), predicts better than the feature model (#32–#34): the 'count' of the organising idea is now a fitted rule.
Step C: the night gain holds at matched count and prior wake (#14b Established); no light step beyond the smooth daily curve (#35).
Superseded by j.core.r6 (Steps D–E: the rules reproduce daily totals without a budget; #43).

nodes.title: Rules that carry history generate the daily sleep without a budget; a REM repayment appears only after handling
nodes.text: Established: REM entry is set by one count of NREM since the last REM (emptied by REM, fading over a wake), read through a daily curve (smooth, with no light switch: candidate, #35) that lowers entry about three-fold at night at the same count and prior wake; brief wakes keep the history, wakes ≥ 7 min are not resumed; simulated from these rules, conditional on the observed long wakes and gaps, the model reproduces daily REM and NREM and their day-to-day variation without any budget (#40), and beats a momentum model (#41); an NREM homeostat adds nothing to NREM endings (#42). Candidate: REM missed before a morning round is repaid by a process the rules do not contain, seen only after handled interruptions (#43); handling, dawn timing and the round's sleep loss are not separated, and a general slow REM deficit is neither shown nor excluded (low power). The budget is not needed for the daily totals but was never fitted ('there is no REM budget' is forbidden). Interpretation still to test: only REM entry is regulated. Not testable here: a neural scheduler.

changes.what: Fable conflict review M1: 'read through a smooth daily curve' inside the Established sentence bundled #35 (Candidate); reworded to 'a daily curve (smooth, with no light switch: candidate, #35)'. Verdicts unchanged.

nodes.title: Step F H7 / H8 / H10: is REM maintenance (bout duration, exits) unregulated, as 'only REM entry is regulated' requires?
nodes.text: H7: ln REM-bout duration on the count at onset, dark, ln prior wake, temperature and group size (the planned C3 that was never run). H8: share of REM bouts ending in WAKE vs NREM, night vs day at matched duration. H10: are sequential cycles rarer at night through the gain or through interruptions (second REM within 135 s vs MA count). Sequence-only; pass rules as in the plan; pass2med for night vs day.

outcomes.if: No predictor of REM-bout duration or REM exits holds (scoped negatives, both scorings)
outcomes.then: 'Only REM entry is regulated' moves from proposed to a candidate pattern; REM maintenance is unregulated within these inputs.

outcomes.if: A named predictor (phase, count, temperature, group size) holds for duration or exits
outcomes.then: REM maintenance is regulated too; the organising idea is rewritten and the simulator's history-free REM exits need a term.

nodes.text: The current state and the quantities accumulated since the last REM capture the predictive gain; distant windows add nothing within records. Fragmentation is borderline. nodes.title: One running count since the last REM, with the current state, carries the history; fragmentation adds nothing beyond it

nodes.title: REM propensity builds with NREM accumulated since the last REM (refractory build-up)
nodes.text: Mice and humans: a refractory period after REM, then rising REM propensity (Park 2021, Bassi 2009, Ginsberg 2024).

nodes.title: Deeper recent NREM favours REM; shallow NREM favours waking
Wake accumulated since the last REM lowers the REM drive (REM pressure dissipates in wake)
nodes.text: The predictive fact (v2 #2, candidate): the more wake since the last REM, the less likely an NREM bout ends in REM. This hypothesis reads it as a lower REM drive.

Daily REM 1.683 vs 1.694 h, SD 0.343 vs 0.342 (FINAL); REM share day / night 17.4 / 7.3 vs 17.4 / 6.8 %; latencies 5/6 cells (fail: night after 7–30-min wakes, FINAL, 14 episodes). Carry-over curve: same sign in every bin with a clear observed effect. Night → day slope with day fixed effects (within day, between animals; the pre-registered term): NREM simulated −0.13 / −0.09 vs observed −0.12 / −0.10; REM inside the simulated range on both scorings. v1 → v2 correction: short wakes are sampled with their next state (12–15 % of REM bouts follow a ≤ 10-s wake).

conflicts.title: Does a longer REM lengthen the following NREM interval?

sides.says: Single cycles: +0.07 [0.05, 0.10], 6/6; all cycles +0.01 (n.s.); pre-post-rule states −0.12.
Phase 1 cycles-ahead k = 1 (all REM cycles in a SLEEP, intervening terms controlled): −0.05 (n.s.), 3/6 — 'the classic k = 1 relation is not reproduced'.
Transition model: previous REM length adds a little (−0.31 %), sign depends on the other history terms; null in v1.

conflicts.resolution: Different quantities: where comparable (all cycles), v1 (+0.01) and Phase 1 k = 1 (−0.05) agree on ≈ 0; +0.07 is the single-cycle subset and −0.12 another scoring; v2 #4 is a hazard coefficient conditional on the window terms (+0.13 in M1, −0.04 in M2), not an interval claim. Sayable: v1 #8's allowed wording plus #18. Settling it needs the two-part rerun on three scorings (n.rem_length_two_part).
conflicts.resolved_by: Fable review r1 (v1 audit:43, Phase 1:75, v2 report:33 and 59)

conflicts.title: Does a long wake delay the next REM, given that REM minutes after a wake do not depend on its length?

sides.says: NREM before the first REM after a wake ≥ 7 min grows with ln(wake length): +0.26, 6/6 (cycles that reached REM).
REM minutes over 1–3 h after natural wakes do not depend on wake length on the same events (−0.08, n.s.).

conflicts.resolution: Compatible, not a conflict: different events (≥ 7 min vs mostly 2–7-min wakes), outcomes and selection. Arithmetic from the reported numbers (not a result): +0.26 per ln unit ≈ 3 min per doubling of a ~15-min first-REM latency ≈ 0.3 min less REM in the first hour, which the same-events null (−0.08 [−0.25, +0.09]) cannot detect. n.survival_long_wake measures both on the same events.
conflicts.resolved_by: Fable review r1 (Phase 2:24-27, Phase 3:130 and 151, Phase 3b:18)
conflicts.note: r2: #6 was split; the delay is now #6b (at night only) and the logic audit reads #6 and #12 as consistent (the hour after a long wake also carries extra NREM).

conflicts.title: Do the 10 min–3 h windows carry history beyond the since-last-REM quantities?

sides.says: v2: window terms (10 / 60 / 180 min) add −1.00 % on top of the clock baseline M0; ≈ −0.75 % beyond the anchors (no CI).
Phase 1: bands 10–720 min add +0.12 % [−0.05, +0.32] on top of the since-last-REM layer L2.

conflicts.resolution: Within precision the bands' information is a subset of L2's: they help on top of the current state alone (M3_720 vs M1 −0.40 %, holds) but not on top of L2. v2's 10-min window is Phase 1's current state (L1). The schedule audit supersedes v2 where they differ.

conflicts.title: How large is the night's REM-entry gain at matched prior wake — 'about half' or 'about a third'?
conflicts.resolution: Different quantities, both correct. 'About a third' is the per-step REM-entry rate at the same count and prior wake (C1: OR 0.36 / 0.30; clock ratio 0.37 / 0.34); 'about half' is the model-free REM bouts per NREM hour after equally short wakes, count not matched (A3: 0.41 / 0.52).
